Yes. For a single-location Toronto gym, I’d keep the first test fairly lean and pay for measurable acquisition rather than a big “full-service marketing” package.

Affordable options worth investigating

Jeff Social Marketing — Toronto-based and positioned as a budget-conscious digital marketing provider. It could be worth getting a quote if you want hands-on social/website help.

SET Marketing — Toronto agency with a fitness/wellness focus and an emphasis on tracking revenue rather than just social metrics.

Marketing For You — Toronto-based, with paid search, SEO, social and analytics; potentially useful if you primarily need lead generation rather than elaborate branding.

H2O Digital Marketing Inc. — GTA-based and offers broader digital marketing, though I'd ask specifically for a small-gym package before assuming it's affordable.

For a gym-specialist option, Attribute Media publishes unusually concrete pricing: its gym program starts at $600/month, with ad spend separate. It reports an average $22 lead across its gym clients and says 20–40% of leads become members, although those are its own client figures rather than independent Toronto benchmarks. 
Attribute Media

SearchPod publishes $600/month minimum for Google/Meta management and $500/month for its local-SEO offering, both month-to-month. 
SearchPod

What I'd budget

A sensible initial test might look like:

Item	Monthly starting point
Marketing management	$500–$1,000
Meta/Google ad spend	$750–$1,500
Total	$1,250–$2,500

You don't necessarily need both Google and Meta on day one. For many gyms, I'd test one strong offer + one channel + good follow-up before expanding.

Realistic membership expectations

Be skeptical of anyone promising “30 new members a month” without knowing your gym's price, neighbourhood, capacity, offer and existing conversion rate.

Published fitness benchmarks vary considerably. One 2026 dataset reports Meta leads around $30 and Google leads around $62, with lead-to-member conversion ranging from 18–44% across the fitness locations it studied. 
Rogolook
 Another gym-focused provider reports roughly $22/lead and 20–40% lead-to-member conversion among its own clients. 
Attribute Media

So, as a planning scenario rather than a promise, suppose you spend $1,000 on ads:

$30–$60 per lead → roughly 17–33 leads

20–30% eventually join → roughly 3–10 new memberships

Then subtract cancellations/churn to determine net membership growth

That's why I'd judge an agency on cost per acquired member, not clicks, impressions or even cheap leads.

And don't overlook the sales process. A gym case study published by one agency went from 18% to 29% trial-to-member conversion after changing its campaigns, landing page and follow-up—not simply by buying more advertising. 
Big AL Consulting

The offer I'd ask agencies to build around

Instead of advertising “Join our gym,” I'd test something concrete such as:

“7-Day Gym Trial + Fitness Assessment — $X”

or, for a more coaching-oriented gym:

“3 Personal Training Sessions + Gym Access — $X.”

Then track:

Ad → enquiry → booked trial → attended trial → membership → 30/90-day retention.

If an agency can't show you those numbers, I'd be cautious about paying them.

If you tell me the gym's monthly membership price, neighbourhood, approximate current membership, and monthly marketing budget, I can work out a realistic new-members-per-month target and maximum customer-acquisition cost for the gym.
